blocks.text: Matrix multiplication is where scalars, vectors, matrices, and the dot product from earlier in this module all come together at once. It looks intimidating written out as a full grid of numbers, but every single cell of the result is nothing more than a dot product, already fully covered in an earlier lesson.

blocks.alt: Matrix A and matrix B combining through multiplication into a result matrix
blocks.caption: This lesson covers exactly how this combination actually works.

blocks.text: This is a good example of a rule that feels arbitrary when memorized in isolation but becomes obvious the moment it is traced back to something already understood, here, the simple requirement that a dot product needs two equally sized vectors.
1. The Shape Rule

Two matrices can only be multiplied together if the number of columns in the first exactly matches the number of rows in the second. A matrix of shape (m, n) times a matrix of shape (n, p) produces a result of shape (m, p), the shared n disappearing from the final shape entirely.

blocks.alt: Matrix A of shape m by n times matrix B of shape n by p equals a result of shape m by p, with the two n values needing to match
blocks.caption: The inner two numbers must agree; the outer two numbers survive into the shape of the result.

code.content:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])   # shape (2, 3)
B = np.array([[7, 8], [9, 10], [11, 12]])   # shape (3, 2)
result = A.dot(B)
print(result.shape)   # (2, 2)

blocks.text: This rule is worth testing against the matrix addition lesson rule too, for contrast: addition required both matrices to share the exact same shape, while multiplication only requires one specific pair of numbers, the inner dimensions, to match, which is a genuinely different and, at first, less intuitive requirement.

It is worth practicing reading shapes quickly from just the numbers alone, given (4, 7) and (7, 2), the result will be (4, 2), given (7, 4) and (7, 2), the multiplication is not even valid in that order at all, since 4 does not match 7.
1.1 Why the Inner Dimensions Must Match

Every entry of the result comes from a dot product between a row of the first matrix and a column of the second, and a dot product is only defined between two vectors of the exact same length, covered in the dot product lesson. A row from A and a column from B can only be dotted together if they hold the same number of values, which is exactly what the shared n guarantees.

It is worth restating this using the row-times-column picture directly: a row from A has exactly n numbers in it, one per column of A, and a column from B has exactly n numbers in it, one per row of B. The dot product between them only makes sense at all if those two counts genuinely agree.
1.2 Element-Wise Multiplication Is a Different Operation

NumPy plain * operator on two matrices does something entirely different from .dot(): it multiplies matching positions directly, the matrix equivalent of the scalar broadcasting covered in the first lesson of this module, and it requires the two matrices to have the exact same shape, not the inner-matching-outer rule covered here.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(A * B)        # element-wise: [[5 12] [21 32]]
print(A.dot(B))     # matrix multiplication: [[19 22] [43 50]]

blocks.title: Two operations, two different names
blocks.content: Element-wise multiplication is sometimes called the Hadamard product to avoid confusion with matrix multiplication. Whenever code multiplies two matrices, it is worth double checking which of the two operations was actually intended.

blocks.text: Element-wise multiplication does still require both matrices to share the exact same shape, the same strict requirement covered for addition, which is one more useful way to tell the two operations apart quickly: matrix multiplication has a flexible, inner-matching shape rule, while element-wise multiplication demands an exact match, just like addition does.
2. Computing One Entry: A Row Times A Column
To get any single cell of the result, take the matching row from the first matrix, take the matching column from the second matrix, and compute their dot product.

blocks.alt: A specific row of matrix A and a specific column of matrix B being combined into a single cell of the result matrix
blocks.caption: Every cell of the result is produced this exact same way, one row-column pair at a time.

blocks.text: This also explains why the result has exactly m rows and p columns: there are m rows available in the first matrix and p columns available in the second, and every possible pairing of one row with one column produces exactly one entry of the result.

Every one of these row-column dot products is entirely independent of every other one, which is precisely the property that lets modern hardware compute enormous numbers of them simultaneously rather than one after another, the deeper reason batching, covered later in this lesson, produces such a dramatic speed improvement.
2.1 A Slower, Fully Manual Version

Reading through this manual version once is worth the time, since it makes the row-times-column pattern completely explicit: the innermost loop is exactly the dot product covered in an earlier lesson, run once for every combination of a row from A and a column from B.

Comparing the running time of this manual triple-nested loop version against a single call to a library matrix multiplication function on a reasonably large matrix is a genuinely eye opening exercise, the difference is routinely a hundred times or more, entirely due to how heavily optimized library implementations are for exactly this operation.
3. A Full Worked Example By Hand
Multiplying two small 2 by 2 matrices, step by step, makes the pattern completely concrete.

code.content:
A = [[1, 2],
     [3, 4]]
B = [[5, 6],
     [7, 8]]

# top-left of result: row 1 of A dot column 1 of B
# (1*5 + 2*7) = 19
# top-right: row 1 of A dot column 2 of B
# (1*6 + 2*8) = 22
# bottom-left: row 2 of A dot column 1 of B
# (3*5 + 4*7) = 43
# bottom-right: row 2 of A dot column 2 of B
# (3*6 + 4*8) = 50

result = np.array(A).dot(np.array(B))
print(result)
# [[19 22]
#  [43 50]]

blocks.text: Working through this once by hand, even though real code always uses a library function, is worth the few minutes it takes. It removes any mystery from what dot appears to be doing, since every single entry in the output can be traced back to one specific row and one specific column being multiplied and summed.

It is worth redoing this same calculation using the fully manual function from just above, confirming it produces the identical result as both the hand-computed version and the built-in NumPy call, three different routes to the exact same answer.

Notice this hand calculation took four separate dot product computations, one per cell of the 2 by 2 result, a small enough number to work through on paper, but a useful reminder that a much larger matrix multiplication is doing the exact same thing many more times over.
4. Order Matters: AB Is Not BA
Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Swapping the order can change the result entirely, and it can even make the multiplication undefined if the shapes no longer line up in the swapped order.

It is worth explicitly checking, before assuming AB and BA are even both defined at all, whether the shapes actually allow multiplication in the reversed order. A matrix of shape (2, 3) times one of shape (3, 2) works in that order and produces a (2, 2) result, but multiplying them in the reverse order gives a completely different (3, 3) result, not simply a different version of the same answer.
4.1 When Shapes Make Reversal Impossible

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])   # (2, 3)
B = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]])  # (3, 2)
print(A.dot(B).shape)   # (2, 2), valid
# B.dot(A) would need B columns (2) to match A rows (2), which works here,
# but the result shape (3, 3) is completely different from A.dot(B) shape (2, 2)

blocks.text: This kind of shape mismatch producing a valid but entirely different sized result, rather than an obvious error, is exactly why checking shapes carefully before and after a multiplication is worth the small habit it costs, a silently wrong shape is often more dangerous than a loud crash.
5. Matrix Times Vector: A Special Case

A vector is just a matrix with one column, covered in the scalars, vectors, and matrices lesson, so multiplying a matrix by a vector is the exact same operation, just with p equal to 1. This is precisely the W.dot(x) computation from that earlier neural network layer example.

code.content:
W = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])   # shape (2, 2)
x = np.array([2, 1])              # shape (2,), treated as (2, 1)
print(W.dot(x))                   # [2 1]

blocks.text: This special case is worth recognizing on sight in real code, since a matrix multiplied by something that looks like a plain list of numbers is almost always this exact operation, one dot product per row of the matrix, producing one number per row in the output.

It is worth reading the shape rule from the first section against this specific case directly: a matrix of shape (m, n) times a vector treated as shape (n, 1) produces a result of shape (m, 1), a column vector, exactly matching the general rule with p simply equal to 1.

Recognizing this special case immediately, rather than re-deriving the general rule every time, is genuinely useful since it is by far the most common shape of matrix multiplication encountered in everyday neural network code, one weight matrix acting on one input vector, or one batch of input vectors, at a time.
6. Batches: Multiplying Many Inputs at Once

The real reason matrix multiplication matters so much for performance is that it processes an entire batch of inputs in one single operation. Instead of running one input vector through a layer at a time, an entire matrix of inputs, one row per example, gets multiplied through in one call.

code.content:
X = np.array([[2, 1], [0, 3], [1, 1]])   # 3 examples, each 2 numbers, shape (3, 2)
W = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])            # shape (2, 2)
outputs = X.dot(W)
print(outputs.shape)   # (3, 2), one output row per input example

blocks.title: Why this matters for speed
blocks.content: GPUs are built specifically to perform this kind of large matrix multiplication extremely fast in parallel, which is exactly why training and running neural networks in batches, rather than one example at a time, is dramatically faster in practice.

blocks.text: 6.2 What Happens Without Batching

code.content:
# One example at a time, in a loop
outputs = []
for row in X:
    outputs.append(W.dot(row))
outputs = np.array(outputs)

# The same result, computed in a single batched call instead
outputs_batched = X.dot(W)
print(np.array_equal(outputs, outputs_batched))   # True

blocks.text: Both versions above compute the identical mathematical result, the difference is purely about how efficiently the underlying hardware can execute the computation, not about correctness.

This is a genuinely important practical lesson beyond the pure mathematics: two pieces of code can be mathematically equivalent while differing enormously in real-world running time, and recognizing when a loop can be replaced with a single batched matrix operation is one of the most valuable, immediately applicable skills this lesson offers.
6.1 Numbers Behind the Speedup

Running one thousand input vectors through a layer one at a time means one thousand separate small matrix-vector multiplications, each with its own overhead of launching the computation. Stacking all one thousand inputs into a single matrix and running one matrix-matrix multiplication instead does the exact same total amount of arithmetic, but pays that launch overhead only once, which is where most of the real-world speedup comes from on modern hardware.
7. Associativity, But Not Commutativity

Grouping does not matter, (AB)C always equals A(BC), even though the order of A, B, and C themselves cannot be swapped. This lets a chain of matrix multiplications be computed in whichever grouping happens to be cheapest, without changing the final answer.

This grouping freedom is exactly what makes chaining layers, covered in the scalars, vectors, and matrices lesson, work smoothly. Multiple weight matrices chained together can be reasoned about, and in some cases even precomputed, in whichever order is most convenient, without changing what the network ultimately computes.

It is worth verifying this with actual matrices at least once rather than trusting the rule purely by name, computing both groupings of a three-matrix product and confirming NumPy returns identical results either way.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[2, 0], [1, 2]])
C = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 1]])
left = (A.dot(B)).dot(C)
right = A.dot(B.dot(C))
print(np.array_equal(left, right))   # True

blocks.text: 8. A Worked Example
9. Practice: Multiply These by Hand
Try multiplying [[1, 0], [0, 1]] by [[3, 4], [5, 6]] by hand before checking below.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The first matrix is the identity matrix, covered in its own lesson shortly, and multiplying by it always returns the other matrix completely unchanged. The result is exactly [[3, 4], [5, 6]].

blocks.text: 10. A Second Practice Problem
Try multiplying [[2, 0], [0, 3]] by [[1, 4], [2, 1]] by hand before checking below.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The first matrix is diagonal, which makes this easier than the general case: each row of the result is simply the matching row of the second matrix scaled by the diagonal entry. Row 1 becomes [2, 8], scaled by 2, and row 2 becomes [0, 3], scaled by 3, giving [[2, 8], [0, 3]].

blocks.text: Diagonal matrices like this one are worth recognizing on sight specifically because they make multiplication this easy, a genuinely useful shortcut for building intuition before tackling a fully general, non-diagonal example.
11. Common Mistakes

items: Multiplying two matrices whose inner dimensions do not match and expecting NumPy to figure it out anyway.
Assuming AB equals BA, matrix multiplication almost never commutes.
Confusing matrix multiplication with element-wise multiplication, which multiplies matching positions directly rather than computing dot products.
Forgetting that a matrix times a vector is just the matrix-times-matrix case with one column, and treating it as a separate rule to memorize.

blocks.text: Nearly every one of these mistakes is caught immediately by the simple habit of writing down, or printing, the shapes of both matrices before attempting the multiplication, the exact same defensive habit recommended in the matrix addition lesson, just applied to a stricter and less forgiving rule.
Key Takeaway

Matrix multiplication is only defined when the inner dimensions match, producing a result whose shape is the two outer dimensions. Every single cell of that result is a dot product between a row of the first matrix and a column of the second, the exact same operation covered in the dot product lesson, just applied systematically across every row and column pair.

This operation is not commutative, order and grouping both matter in specific ways, and it is the computational core of every neural network layer, especially once inputs are processed in batches, which is exactly why GPUs, built for fast large-scale matrix multiplication, are the hardware of choice for training and running these models.

Of every operation covered so far in this Math and Statistics module, matrix multiplication is worth the most repeated practice, since a genuinely large share of everything covered later, from covariance matrices to the transformer attention mechanism, is built directly on top of this exact operation.
